799.title: Peacocks and cranes
799.hook: the monks' monsoon poems: clouds, peacocks crying, cranes flying home
799.howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns still keep the rains retreat, vassa, staying in one monastery for the rainy season, and lay people often visit them then with food and robes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subhuti's kuti was roofed, and he told the sky to go ahead. Your line was rain if you like. Today, the rain arrives, and the birds come with it.

Dark clouds stack up over the hills. Thunder. A flash of white as birds lift off a riverbank. In the trees, a peacock cries out. Some of the brothers' songs begin right there, at the edge of the rains. The poets aren't describing the weather to pass the time. They're telling you where they sat, and what the season did to the mind.
screen: `CLOUDS OVER THE HILLS.` → `A PEACOCK CRIES OUT.` → `WHAT THE MONKS DID WITH IT.`

segments.voice: First, the peacocks. In one elder's verses, peacocks with fine crests and blue necks cry out in the woods, the sky rumbles, and the wide earth is soaked with new rain. And then he says: this is the time to meditate. The noise isn't a distraction. It's a signal. Second, the cranes. Another elder, Sappaka, watches a crane with bright white wings take flight from a black storm cloud, afraid of it, looking for shelter. Then, he says, the river Ajakarani delights him. He comes back to that line again and again as the birds come and go, like a song's refrain. Third, the season itself. When the rains come, roads turn to mud, and tradition says the Buddha asked the monks to stop wandering for the rainy months and stay in one place. That stay is called vassa, the rains retreat. So the monsoon poems are poems of staying put. The clouds move, the birds move, the river rises. The monk doesn't go anywhere. Fourth, what these two poems leave out. They don't call the storm holy, or a trap. They don't argue with it. They watch. A bird flies for cover. A river runs high. A man under a roof hears it all and settles a little deeper. The rains came. For these elders, that was enough to begin.
screen: `PEACOCKS CRY: TIME TO MEDITATE.` · `A WHITE CRANE FLEES THE BLACK CLOUD.` · `VASSA: STAY PUT FOR THE RAINS.` · `THEY DON'T ARGUE. THEY WATCH.` · then, large: `THE RAINS CAME.`

segments.voice: Go to a window, step outside, or just close your eyes and feel the air, and watch what the sky is doing without calling it good or bad. If a bird crosses, follow it until it's gone; if a sound comes, a car, a gust, a door, let it be the peacock's cry, a signal to come back to the breath. And stay where you are, the way the monks stayed for the rains.
Vassa. The rains, and the rains retreat: the season behind the brothers' rain songs, peacocks crying as the clouds come in, a white crane flying for shelter ahead of the storm. Today's word.
Your line: the rains came. The monks stayed put, and watched. That's day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: The flower-sweeper's song
800.hook: Sunita, once despised, is honored by gods and people (Theragatha, Sunita)
800.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often tell Sunita's story, and the Buddha's closing words to him, when they teach that what makes a person noble is conduct, not birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peacocks cried and a white crane flew ahead of the storm, in the vassa. Your line was the rains came. Today, a man people didn't want to look at.

Two crowds, one at each end of a single poem. At the start, the Buddha walks into the city with a company of monks around him, and a man who hauls away withered flowers sets down his carrying pole. At the end, that same man sits with a company of gods around him. This is Sunita, met a few weeks ago on that street, hearing the two words that made him a monk: come, monk. Today, the night, and the dawn.
screen: `TWO CROWDS IN ONE POEM.` → `MET BEFORE, ON THE STREET.` → `TODAY, THE NIGHT AND THE DAWN.`

segments.voice: First, the night. After the street, Sunita goes into the forest alone and does what the Teacher told him, without slacking. His song walks through the night watch by watch. In the first watch, he says, he remembered his former lives. In the middle watch, his divine eye was made clear. In the last, he split apart the mass of darkness. Second, the dawn. At sunrise, Indra and Brahma come to him and bow with joined palms. The man who once bowed to everyone is now the one bowed to. They speak: homage to you, finest of men, whose taints are destroyed; you are worthy of offerings. Offerings are what people bring, and this was a man who once lived on little to eat. Third, the mirror. When the Buddha sees him, the song says, Sunita is surrounded by a company of gods, the way the Buddha was surrounded by monks on the morning they met. The poem's shape turns all the way round. Fourth, the smile. The Buddha smiles and speaks a verse: by discipline, by the holy life, by restraint and taming oneself, by these one becomes a brahmin; this is the highest brahmin. In the world of the poem, brahmin names the priestly families, honored by birth. Here it names a way of living. And Sunita doesn't gloat over the people who once looked past him. He just tells it in order: the flowers, the street, the night, the dawn.
screen: `THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.` · `INDRA AND BRAHMA BOW AT DAWN.` · `NOW HE STANDS AMONG THE GODS.` · `THE BUDDHA SMILES: A BRAHMIN BY CONDUCT.` · then, large: `ONCE DESPISED.`

segments.voice: Picture someone whose work happens before you arrive or after you leave: the person who unlocks the building, the night shift at the hospital, whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen. See the hours they keep, the dark before dawn, and in your mind put your palms together, the way Indra and Brahma did for Sunita at sunrise. If a judgment rises, notice it, and come back to the breath.

Your line: once despised. By dawn, the man people looked past was called worthy of offerings. Eight hundred days now, each one counted.

801.title: The one who stopped
801.hook: Angulimala's song: whoever was careless and now is not lights up the world like the moon (Theragatha, Angulimala)
801.howItsDone: In some Theravada countries, monks chant the Angulimala paritta, a protective verse from his story, for women in childbirth, and teachers tell his story when they speak of beginning again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sunita the flower-sweeper, bowed to at dawn by gods and called dakkhineyya. Your line was once despised. Today, a man who wasn't looked down on. He was feared.

I have stopped. You stop too. In the old story, those are the Buddha's words to a man running after him with a sword. The man is Angulimala, the bandit named for the garland of fingers he wore. In the sutta he runs as hard as he can and still can't catch up, though the Buddha is only walking. He shouts at him to stop, and gets that answer back. That chase is told in the Middle Length Discourses. Today, the song the Theragatha gives to Angulimala himself, after he stopped.
screen: `I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO.` → `HE RUNS AND CAN'T CATCH UP.` → `TODAY, HIS OWN SONG.`

segments.voice: First, his name. My name was Harmless, he says, even while I was harming. Now the name is true. I harm no one. The old name had been false. Now it fits. Second, the turn. He looks back on himself as a bandit, swept along like something in a flood, and says he went to the Buddha for refuge. He doesn't dress it up. Third, the line he's remembered for. Whoever was careless before, and afterward is not, lights up the world like the moon set free from a cloud. The same verse stands in the Dhammapada, and Max Müller's old translation gives it like this: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." The clouds were real. The moon doesn't pretend they weren't there. It comes out from behind them. Fourth, the cost. In the sutta, after he becomes a monk, Angulimala goes for alms and people throw clods and stones. He comes back bleeding, his bowl broken, his robe torn. The Buddha tells him to bear it: the fruit of what he did is ripening now, here. So the moon from the cloud isn't a clean slate. It's a turning point, and then a road. Some readers ask whether the story comes too easily, and what of the people he hurt. The text doesn't hide from that. It keeps the light and the stones in the same story.
screen: `HARMLESS: NOW THE NAME IS TRUE.` · `SWEPT ALONG, THEN TAKING REFUGE.` · `THE MOON SET FREE FROM A CLOUD.` · `STONES ON THE ALMS ROUND.` · then, large: `THE MOON FROM THE CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Let one recent, ordinary thing come to mind that you'd like to have done differently, a sharp word, a dropped promise, not the worst thing. Don't pretend it didn't happen, since the clouds were real; just stop, the way Angulimala stopped. Then, on an out-breath, let a small next step come into view, like the moon coming out, without needing to take it yet.
Angulimala. The bandit named for a garland of fingers, who stopped running after the Buddha, became a monk, and sang of the moon set free from a cloud. Today's word.
Your line: the moon from the cloud. Harmless became a true name at last. Until tomorrow.

802.title: The actor's longing
802.hook: Talaputa, an actor turned monk, talks to his own restless mind (Theragatha, Talaputa)
802.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in several Buddhist traditions encourage students to meet a wandering mind with patience rather than harshness, and some point to Talaputa's song as an early example of speaking to one's own mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Angulimala stopped, and the moon came out from the cloud. Your line was the moon from the cloud. Today, a monk who keeps asking himself one word: when.

When. It's a word for waiting rooms, long drives, the last hour before the weekend. In one of the long songs in the brothers' book, an actor says it to himself over and over. Talaputa led a troupe of players. In a sutta, he asks the Buddha what becomes of actors who make crowds laugh with truth and lies. The Buddha would rather not answer, then does, and Talaputa weeps, and asks to go forth. In his song, he talks to his own mind.
screen: `WHEN.` → `AN ACTOR ASKS ABOUT ACTORS.` → `HE TALKS TO HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: First, the longing. His song opens with a run of questions. When will I live alone in mountain caves? When will I wear the rag robe and want nothing? When will I see clearly that it all passes? The Pali word is kada, and it comes back so often it becomes the poem's rhythm. Second, the turn. Further on, the questions stop, and he speaks to the mind directly, as if it were someone sitting across from him. You're the one who urged me into this life, he says, and now you pull the other way. Third, the tone. It isn't only scolding. He reasons with the mind. He coaxes it. He reminds it of the forest, the rain, the calling birds, the quiet it said it wanted. Some readers hear an actor's craft in it: one man playing two parts on one stage, the restless mind and the patient monk, trading lines. Fourth, the ordinary day. Talaputa doesn't pretend the restless mind belongs to someone else. He also doesn't simply do what it says. He talks to it like someone he has to live with, and his song doesn't pretend one talking-to settles it. Verse after verse, the longing stays honest, and the conversation goes on. Perhaps that's what an actor brought to the forest: the knack of hearing your own voice as one voice among several, and answering it.
screen: `A RUN OF QUESTIONS: WHEN?` · `HE SPEAKS TO THE MIND DIRECTLY.` · `SCOLDING, REASONING, COAXING.` · `TWO PARTS ON ONE STAGE.` · then, large: `WHEN WILL IT BE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the mind do what it does; when it wanders, and it will, speak to it the way you'd speak to a restless friend in the passenger seat: there you are, come back now. Talaputa scolded and coaxed, so try only the coaxing, and notice whether a kind voice brings the mind home faster than a hard one.
Kada. When: the word Talaputa the actor-turned-monk asks again and again, speaking to his own restless mind. Today's word.
Your line: when will it be. Even a restless mind can be talked to kindly. Day eight hundred two, done.

803.title: Kassapa's mountains
803.hook: the old ascetic loves the rocky hills, the rain, the elephants (Theragatha, Mahakassapa)
803.howItsDone: Forest monasteries in the Theravada tradition are often set in hills and woods, and teachers read Mahakassapa's verses as a picture of how simple living and delight in nature go together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Talaputa the actor asked kada, when, and talked to his own mind. Your line was when will it be. Today, an old monk who isn't waiting for anything. He's already where he loves to be.

Rocky slopes. Clear, cool water. Elephants trumpeting somewhere below. Rain sweeping over the ridge. It could be a postcard, but it's a run of pictures from the verses the Theragatha gives to Mahakassapa, the stern elder met earlier this year, whom tradition remembers for the strict practices: rag robes, plain food, the forest. Today he does something softer. In his own song, he tells you what he loves.
screen: `ROCK, WATER, ELEPHANTS, RAIN.` → `THE STERN ELDER.` → `TODAY, WHAT HE LOVES.`

segments.voice: First, the refrain. After each picture of the hills, Kassapa says the same thing: those rocky hills delight me. Again, and again. The elder known for doing without is, in his own words, full of delight. Second, what's in the hills. Streams of clear, cool water. Slopes where elephants pass. The calls of birds. Rain on the rock. Room to sit alone. Nothing on that list is a luxury, and none of it belongs to him. Third, why the hills. His verses open by warning against going about surrounded by a crowd, where the mind gets pulled this way and that. The hills are the other side of that warning: where he can practice. So the delight isn't instead of the discipline. It grows right out of it. Fourth, the kind of joy it is. Not the joy of owning a view. Kassapa doesn't speak of owning anything up there. He comes, he sits, the rain falls, he goes down for alms and comes back. Some readers are surprised that a man of strict habits sings about beauty at all. The poem doesn't seem to feel any tension in it. A hard life can still have a place it loves, and say so without embarrassment. These hills delight me isn't a confession. It's simple news from the ridge.
screen: `THE REFRAIN: THOSE HILLS DELIGHT ME.` · `WATER, ELEPHANTS, RAIN, ROOM TO SIT.` · `AWAY FROM THE CROWD.` · `DELIGHT WITHOUT OWNING.` · then, large: `THESE HILLS DELIGHT ME.`

segments.voice: Find a hill outside your window, or bring one to mind, a slope you climbed as a kid, a ridge from a trip, the mound in a park, and see its shape: the rock, the grass, the sky behind it. Let the breath slow to the pace of something that doesn't move. When the mind wanders, come back to the hill; it hasn't gone anywhere.
Kassapa's mountains. The rocky hills the stern elder sang about: cool water, rain, elephants, room to sit alone, and his refrain that they delight him. Today's word.
Your line: these hills delight me. A strict life and a glad heart sat on the same ridge. See you tomorrow.

804.title: Sariputta's calm
804.hook: the wise one's verses: I don't long for death, I don't long for life (Theragatha, Sariputta)
804.carry: as a servant waits for wages
804.howItsDone: Theravada teachers sometimes recite Sariputta's lines about not longing for death or life when speaking of how a freed person meets the end, and they are read at some reflections on death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kassapa's rocky hills, and his refrain that they delighted him. Your line was these hills delight me. Today, the wise one, and the way he waits.

Payday. The work is already done. The money will come when it comes. A worker who's finished doesn't stand at the door all week waiting for it, and doesn't forget about it either. Sariputta, the disciple tradition remembers for his wisdom, reaches for that very picture in his verses: a hired worker, waiting for his wages. It's how he describes waiting for the end of his own life.
screen: `PAYDAY. THE WORK IS DONE.` → `SARIPUTTA, THE WISE ONE.` → `HOW HE WAITS.`

segments.voice: First, the two refusals. Sariputta says: I don't long for death. I don't long for life. He isn't hurrying toward the end, and he isn't clutching at more time. Second, the picture. I wait for my time, he says, as a servant waits for wages, and he adds something that matters: mindful, and clearly knowing. A hired worker who has finished the job isn't chasing the pay as a prize. It's simply what comes next. Sariputta's work, the long training of the mind, is complete. What's left is to wait, awake, without leaning either way. Third, the load. In his verses he says the teacher has been served, the heavy burden laid down, what leads to becoming rooted out. Other elders in the Theragatha close their songs with words like these. It's their way of saying: done. Fourth, why this can unsettle a listener. A line that won't long for life can sound bleak at first. Read in his verses, it sounds closer to ease. He isn't tired of living. He just isn't grasping in either direction. Some readers hear in it the end of fear. Others hear a craftsman's quiet pride in finished work. Either way, the picture is plain: a worker at the end of the day, tools put away, sitting on the step until the pay arrives.
screen: `NO LONGING FOR DEATH, NOR FOR LIFE.` · `LIKE A WORKER WAITING FOR WAGES.` · `THE HEAVY BURDEN LAID DOWN.` · `NOT TIRED. NOT GRASPING.` · then, large: `AS A SERVANT WAITS FOR WAGES.`

segments.voice: Choose something you're waiting on, a reply, a result, a season of life to end or to begin, and hold it in mind, then let go of the handle, neither pulling it closer nor pushing it away. Sit the way a worker sits when the work is done, not watching the door, and each time the mind leans toward the thing, lean back into the breath.
Sariputta's calm. The wise disciple's verses: no longing for death, no longing for life, waiting for his time, mindful, as a worker waits for wages. Today's word.
Your line: as a servant waits for wages. Not hurrying, not clutching, just awake. That's day eight hundred four.

chat.says: What did Sariputta mean, waiting like a worker for his wages?
options: His work was done, so he waited calmly, not grasping either way.
He hoped for a reward in heaven for all his work as a monk.

chat.meaning: Sariputta longs for neither death nor life. His training is complete, so he waits for his time, mindful, like a worker whose job is done.

805.title: Ananda's grief
805.hook: Ananda's verses after the passing: the friend is gone, all directions are dark (Theragatha, Ananda)
805.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often turn to Ananda's grief, and the Buddha's reply about the parting from all that is dear, when they speak with people who are mourning, and some point to his verse on mindfulness of the body as a friend that stays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sariputta waited for his time as a worker waits for wages. Your line was as a servant waits for wages. Today, the one left behind to do the waiting.

All the directions go dark. A friend is gone, the teacher is gone, and the ground goes out from under him. That moment is in the verses of Ananda, the Buddha's attendant. Tradition says he walked beside the teacher for years, looked after his needs, and remembered what he taught. After a run of calm voices, men who have put the burden down, today sits with that moment, and with what he found to hold on to.
screen: `THE GROUND GOES OUT.` → `THE BUDDHA'S ATTENDANT.` → `WHAT HE HELD ON TO.`

segments.voice: First, the line. All the directions are dark, he says. The teachings aren't clear to me. The good friend has gone, and everything seems dark. Second, whose death. The verses speak of a friend gone and of a teacher passed away. Tradition links these lines to the death of Sariputta, whose calm came yesterday, and to the passing of the Buddha. In one sutta, when word of Sariputta's death reaches Ananda, he tells the Buddha that his body feels unsteady, the directions aren't clear to him, and the teachings won't come to mind. Third, what's surprising. This sits in a book of freed men, and here is a long-time follower saying grief has knocked the teaching right out of his head. The collection keeps his words as they are. Fourth, what he does with it. In the same verses, Ananda says that for one whose friend has gone and whose teacher has passed, there's no friend like mindfulness of the body. When the people are gone, what's left to hold is this breath, this body, here. And in the sutta, the Buddha answers him with what he had always taught: everything dear and pleasing will change and be parted from us. How could it be otherwise? He doesn't scold the grief. He reminds Ananda where to stand inside it. In these verses, grief isn't kept out of the practice. It's where the practice goes next.
screen: `ALL THE DIRECTIONS ARE DARK.` · `A FRIEND GONE, A TEACHER GONE.` · `THE BOOK KEEPS HIS WORDS.` · `NO FRIEND LIKE THE BODY'S MINDFULNESS.` · then, large: `ALL DIRECTIONS DARK.`

segments.voice: Let one face come, a friend who's gone, whether they died, moved away or simply drifted, and notice where you feel it, the chest, the throat, behind the eyes, without pushing it off or digging for more. Then, like Ananda, rest some attention in the body itself, the weight in the chair, the breath going in and out: the friend in the mind, the breath in the body. If it gets too heavy, open your eyes and look around the room.
Ananda's grief. The attendant's verses when friend and teacher had gone: all directions dark, and mindfulness of the body as the friend that stays. Today's word.
Your line: all directions dark. Even grief has a place to stand. Go gently; see you tomorrow.

chat.says: Ananda followed the Buddha for years. Why did grief hit him so hard?
options: Losing friend and teacher, all went dark; mindfulness of the body steadied him.
He felt the teacher had left him behind on purpose, and he was hurt.
He grieved because he had never actually learned the teachings well.
chat.meaning: Ananda's verses say all directions went dark. He found no friend like mindfulness of the body, and the Buddha reminded him all that's dear will change.
